image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - Tournament bracket diagram for NCAA basketball, shown separately for **Women’s Bracket** and **Men’s Bracket**.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Side-by-side panels**: two large bracket panels, one for women and one for men.  
   - **Bracket/tree layout**: teams progress through rounds via connected lines.  
   - **Regional subdivision** within each bracket (e.g., Greenville, Seattle, South, East, Midwest, West).  
   - Not stacked; not a standard faceted statistical chart, though the two main panels function like a simple split by tournament.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Tournament division (Women’s / Men’s) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side panel; title text |
| Round | Ordinal | Horizontal position across the bracket; round headers at top |
| Region | Categorical/nominal | Spatial grouping within each bracket; region labels on edges |
| Team name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to bracket positions |
| Seed number | Ordinal | Numeric text preceding team names |
| Team record (wins-losses) | Quantitative | Parenthetical text in first-round team labels |
| Game score / points | Quantitative | Numeric text placed beside teams in each matchup |
| Advancement / winner progression | Categorical/nominal (outcome status) | Connecting bracket lines leading to the next round |
| Champion | Categorical/nominal | Center-most final label/box in each bracket |

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the women's bracket had slightly more predictable teams than the men's. Two number 1 seeds were in the Final Four, and the Championship game was played between the number 2 seed and the number 3 seed. I noticed a few upsets at the beginning of the tournament, but the championship match had the top teams in the country. What's very interesting is that this is the first year since 1985 that Stanford, UCONN, or Tennessee has not been in the Elite Eight. I wonder what this will mean for collegiate women's basketball growth in America. This bracket shows the growth of the game away from just the perennially dominant teams such as UCONN, Stanford, and Tennessee and towards up-and-coming programs such as South Carolina, LSU, and Iowa. The men's bracket had many more upsets, like FDU and Princeton. No number one seed was left in the tournament by the elite eight. The final four for last year’s tournament were Kansas, UNC, Villanova, and Duke, teams that are usually at the top of the NCAA. This year's final four consisted of San Diego State, Florida Atlantic University, UCONN, and Miami. Besides Connecticut, most of these teams rarely advanced to the Elite Eight. How will this affect college basketball and the transfer portal? Will dominant teams in the NCAA change dramatically or gradually? This affects me because I am a fan of men’s and women’s college basketball. My headline is “Crave the Chaos: the Madness of the NCAA March Tournament.”

comments.raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the NCAA Men's and Women's March Madness brackets.  The main thing I notice is how in both brackets, relatively higher seeded teams got to the finals.  In women's, it was 2 seed Iowa and 3 seed LSU, and in the men's it was 5 seed S.D. State and 4 seed Connecticut.  Additionally, the different sides have comparable scores for most games.  There is a good variety of close games, as well as clear wins.  However, one thing that does stand out is how the women's final had a rather high scoring game and the men's final was much lower.  I wonder how exactly they rank all the teams.  Some teams have better records than others, but are still being ranked lower.  Could this be because they played against harder competition or won more games in their division?  This affects me and my community because college basketball is a popular form of entertainment and is something many my age pay a lot of attention to.  I would entitle this graph: "Expanding on March Madness."

comments.raw_comment:
I thought it was interesting how the records didn't determine the rankings for both brackets. Some examples of this includes Charleston being seed 12 with a 31-3 record and SDSU being seed 5 with a worse 27-6 record for the men's side. Similarly, one the women's side, Gardner Webb had a better record than Utah (29-4, 25-4 respectively), but Gardner was ranked 15th and Utah was ranked 2nd.  It was also interesting how that both brackets had the same number of upsets in the round of 64 (7) and similar upsets in the round of 32 (4 for women and 5 for men), the men had a much lower average ranking in the sweet 16 than the women. The men's average ranking is 4.875, while the womens is a 3.69.

One thing I wonder about is how the teams are ranked. As mentioned above, teams with worse records are ranked higher, so I wonder what the algorithm is to determine this. What other factors are in play when determining the team rankings?

This relates to me as I filled out a March Madness bracket myself. While I did pretty poorly, I think brackets are fun, as it provides a light hearted competition and can connect you to the game, even if you don't care about basketball. I personally find sports boring, but I still would constantly check for results and rooting for teams in my bracket.

A headline for this graph could be "Decoding the March Madness"

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at the NCAA bracket results, I noticed that the Men's tournament had many upsets, and top-ranked teams missed the second round. I wonder how many games were decided by pure chance, not from superior skill or talent. For example, San Diego State University had two consecutive game-winning shots in the quarter and semi-finals. If you look at the Women's tournament, the higher-seeded teams generally prevailed hence fewer upsets. For example, seven of the eight teams in the elite were ranked seed five or below. Additionally, I wonder how these outcomes would change if the tournament was longer and each round had a series of games. March Madness was fun to watch because I like playing and watching basketball in general, and I have roommates from San Diego who were San Diego State fans. Overall, this bracket encaptures how the Men's and Women's tournaments unfolded. Each team was assigned a tournament seed from strength of schedule and regular season record. I am excited to watch March Madness again next year!

comments.raw_comment:
What did I notice?:

Something that I noticed first in the women's bracket is that the teams with a high seeding in each group ended up advancing further than the lower-seeded teams in their group bracket.  For example in the final four, the highest seed was 1 and the lowest was 3 which is very impressive.  Most of the scores from both brackets were really close games and there weren't many blowouts.  In the women's bracket, there were also only two games where a team scored over 100 points.  In the men's bracket, there were no games that reached 100.  The highest-scoring game was 98 put up by Kansas State in the game versus Michigan State in the elite eight games for the East group.

What do I wonder?:

I wonder how each team is seeded because initially, I thought it was just the team's record from the season, but it seems like some teams are seeded lower than other teams but they have a better record.  For example in the women's bracket, the Seattle 4 region, Middle Tenn. has a record (28-4) but is seed eleven and Colorado has a record (23-8) as the sixth seed.  

How does this relate to you and your community?:

I do play basketball and watch basketball occasionally.  March Madness is actually something I did watch as it was happening.  I kept up with a few teams and It was fun to see future NBA prospects and these young players going at it with each other.  It's very intense and exciting.

From comparing the final four for both the women's and men's bracket, it's interesting to see the difference in the seeding of the teams. From the women's bracket, the final four consisted of higher seeding teams competing such as seeding #1 through #3, while the men's final four consisted of teams such as Fla. Atlantic, which was seed #9. It is also interesting to see that in both brackets, teams that were seed #1 did not win the championship even though in the women's bracket, two seed #1 teams made it to the final four. What I wondered as I analyzed the brackets was how teams were seeded. In the men's bracket, why is USC seeded in the Eastern region when it should be seeded in the West? Why is Northwestern playing in the Western Conference? Is it because the school is North"west"ern? 

March Madness was very entertaining to watch and engage in since my friends and I would create brackets and predict the winning team. However, my predictions would always fall short since the games are unpredictable and the outcomes are unexpected. Overall, March Madness is a bonding experience between my friends and I and we usually look forward to it every year.

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at the round of 64, I noticed that that was the category that played the outermost ranked teams (rank #1 v rank #16, rank #2 v rank #15, and so on). After observing them I noticed that the more extreme female teams tended to have a larger spread in points compared to the more extreme male teams. After observing this data I recorded the point and averaged the 8 most largest ranked unbalanced games. The mean difference in scores between the 8 sets of women's' games was a point difference of 35.375 points while the mean difference in scores between the 8 sets of men's games was a point difference of 17.375. We can also observe that all of the sampled individual mens game differences fall beneath the women's point difference mean (35.375) and all of the sampled individual women's games fall above the men's point difference mean (17.375).

This makes me wonder why there is such an extreme difference in points. A larger mean difference in points would most likely mean that the variance in skill is higher. (Although my sport's knowledge is limited) I suspect that the higher viewership and profits give incentive for mens basketball to be a more competitive environment leading to a potential smaller variance in point spreads. 

More than half of my friends follow March Madness and enjoy watching the games. Although I am not as invested, it is interesting to see the games as a whole after they have been played through.

Whats going on in this graph?

A Spread in Skills

comments.raw_comment:
One aspect that I took notice of were the number of upsets in both the men and women's brackets. Neither of them had number one seeds in the final, and in the men's bracket the last of the number one seeds were knocked out in the round of 16, so not a single number one seed remained in the last 8 teams of the tournament. 

I wonder how often it is that number one or even two seed make it to the final four, or better.  Something else I'm curious about is how seeds are determined. I know that the team's record plays a big role in that, but an example where even that doesn't hold is when San Diego St. is seeded 5th with a (27-6) record, and they play a 12th seeded Charleston team (31-3). Even though Charleston has 4 more wins, they are seeded 7 places below San Diego St. It would be cool to know how much other factors play into seeding for March Madness. 

As for an impact on the community, I think that all of these upsets and seemingly unpredictable factors that happen in games adds elements of thrill and excitement to make for more attention and viewers during the tournament. 

Headline: (Un)Predictable Madness: Men's and Women's March Madness Brackets

I noticed how there are six rounds of games for the entirety of March Madness for both men’s and women’s basketball, not counting the first four games shown at the bottom of the graphs. They each start with 64 teams, each assigned an initial seed. The men’s bracket is grouped by simple regions while the women’s bracket is grouped by Greenville or Seattle, numbered 1-4. I also noticed that the team’s previous stats were noted next to the team name in the first round, except for almost all the 16 seed teams. However, one 16th seed team beat the 1st seed in the men's bracket, which I thought was interesting. 
I wonder why they match up the teams in the first round the way that they do. It almost seems unfair to set the 16th seed team against the 1st seed team right off the bat. I wonder if it would be better to pair 1 with 9 and 2 with 10 and so on for the first games. Also, I would like to learn what the region grouping means for the women’s bracket, because I could not quite grasp it from the graph. I am also curious about how many people guessed these exact brackets before march madness started. 

This impacts me and my community because my school was not in a league that participated in the displayed March Madness bracket and I wish my school was good enough to be included.

comments.raw_comment:
It's interesting how, in the women's brackets, Virginia Tech and South Carolina both made it to the final four, and they were initially seed #1 in their respective initial divisions. However, neither team advanced to the championship. It's also interesting how the two championship teams were fairly matched in seed levels. Iowa was seed #2, and LSU was seed #3 in their respective initial divisions. A similar thing is seen in the men's bracket, where SD state was seed #5, and Connecticut was seed #4 in their respective initial divisions. It's intriguing to see how the teams that were initially given top-seed values due to their superior performance maintained their performance and were ultimately evenly matched in the final game. However, the teams given the #1 seed value, to begin with, don't seem to make it into the championship. I wonder how often a #1 seeded team makes it to the championship and, moreover, actually becomes champion. 

Being a college student with friends who love and play basketball, this is not the first time I have heard about March Madness. It's fun to recognize a few familiar teams on the bracket, like UCSB and UCLA. Although I am not a diehard basketball fan, joining a community and supporting your peers is fun.
Happy March Madness!

Catchy title: Sowing the Seeds

comments.raw_comment:
What Do you Notice?

I noticed that both graphs have the same general format, with 64 initial teams that are cut in half each round. The seed numbers are also identical because there are four groups of 1-16. I also noticed that the teams are separated into four different regions, which are different for the women’s and men’s brackets. In the men’s bracket, the regions are south, east, midwest, and west. However, in the women’s bracket, they are separated into Greenville 1, Greenville 2, Seattle 3, and Seattle 4.

What do you wonder?

I wonder how the teams are placed into their corresponding seeds. For example, what makes a team have to play in the “First Four” group? Why do they have to play an extra game when the NCAA can just select 64 teams? Also, where are all the games played at? With so many teams and games, they must spread out the games to accommodate everyone. I also wonder how often lower seeds beat the higher seeds in general.

What Impact does this have on you and your community?

I know a lot of people who are into March Madness and like to make brackets before the tournament. Knowing how the tournament works and the structure of the brackets would obviously be an advantage for them. Some people just enjoy watching the games, which typically turn out to be very exciting.

I also notice that there is more to the graph than just the winning teams, there is also additional information about the games and teams at the top and bottom of the graph. What do you wonder?

What impact does this have on you and your community?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that both the men’s and women’s brackets are laid out the same, with the round labels at the top, the label in the center, each team with the respective points and seed per game, and the final match in gray in the center. I also notice that for the women’s team final, the seeds are 2 and 3, which seems very likely. However the men’s final has a fourth and fifth seed, which means there must have been a few upsets during the tournament. 
As someone who does not know much about basketball, I wonder how each team’s seeding and the “First Four'' teams are picked. The “First Four '' interest me because they are all seeds 16 for the left and eleven for the right. I also wonder why the Men’s bracket is separated by a compass point, while the women’s team is separated by either Greenville 1/2 or Seattle 3/4.
As a current college student, I heard a lot of raucous around picking brackets and how most people’s brackets failed after the first few games. While my school isn’t on the list, I know people at SDSU and their whole community were brought together after the men’s basketball team made it to the finals. Seeing a visualization of the final bracket shows me how many first-pick teams had upset and how exciting the season must have been. 
I would title this: “March Madness: A Wild Season Broken Down”.

While I am not a huge basketball fan, plenty of colleges from my state participate in March Madness, thus many fans in my community tune in to support their teams. So, March Madness captures the interest of many in my community.

A catchy title I thought of is "The bracket no one made -- again" as the results of these games are often unpredictable.

comments.raw_comment: I initially noticed that as each team is listed in the Round of 64, next to team name is their standings. The four teams from the First Four that make the top 64 do not have their standings included, but in the Women’s Bracket a fifth team, Norfolk State also does not have standings. In the Men’s Bracket, this does not occur seeing as the only four teams without their standings listed are the four teams from the First Four. One aspect of this graph that is excluded that I believe is critical to include is the year. I know that these brackets are for the 2023 N.C.A.A. basketball tournament, but that is not explicitly stated on the graph. As someone who grew up in the South, college sports are a huge deal. Specifically, college football and basketball. The March Madness bracket is the topic of discussion throughout the entire month of March, so these graphs have a huge impact on my community. As a college student, discussing March Madness brackets and watching the games are some of the most popular activities of the month. This month, more specifically for the men’s basketball, I was completely shocked by several games. Teams in high seeds were losing to much lower seed teams. I think a fitting name for this graph would be “The March Madness Brackets that Drove Fans Mad.”
